item.title: Tau Robotics Deploys Remotely Piloted Humanoid Cleaning Robots in San Francisco
item.description:
Tau Robotics Deploys Remotely Piloted Humanoid Cleaning Robots in San Francisco

I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.

🤖 Overview

  • Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes.
  • The robots are piloted remotely by humans who watch what’s happening via cameras mounted in the robots’ heads and wrists.
  • While cleaning, the robots collect data that Tau will use to train more independent descendants.

🛠️ How it works

  • Human pilots perform motions on a control interface; sensors transmit those movements to the robot, which copies them (kinematic guidance).
  • Tasks that need kinematic guidance include making the bed and folding laundry; these produce especially valuable training data.
  • The robots communicate with Tau’s headquarters through a 3D‑printed “head” with antennae.
  • A short signal transmission delay can affect coordination, causing the robot to walk “strangely.”
  • Overheating of the remote‑operator’s equipment can cause the robot to stall.

⚙️ Robot specifications

  • Height: four‑and‑a‑half‑foot‑tall.
  • 3D‑printed head with antennae for communication.
  • Two 3D‑printed claw “hands” (human‑like hands were found not durable enough).
  • Grippy socks to avoid scratching hardwood floors.
  • Each robot wears a Tau Robotics shirt.

📋 Capabilities

  • Can vacuum and mop without any human help.
  • With kinematic guidance, can make the bed and fold laundry.
  • In a later visit, cleaned a kitchen, tackled a toilet, and re‑attached a cleaning wand three times by poking it into place.
  • Struggles with stairs, often climbing with a “drunk” gait and occasional backward stumbles.

💰 Pricing

  • $30 for an hour‑long cleaning with a single robot (initial offering).
  • $60 per weekly cleaning with two robots (current rate).
  • $100 for a one‑time visit (current rate).
  • Even at $30 per hour, the robots are thorough but slow, making self‑cleaning potentially more efficient.

🚧 Limitations & Incidents

  • Stair navigation is unreliable; the robot can stagger backward.
  • Overheating can cause the robot to stall; in one case the remote‑operator’s equipment shut down.
  • Without remote assistance, the robot cannot clean.
  • The robot is slow, and watching it for the entire visit may not be an efficient use of time.

🚀 Future outlook

  • Tau’s long‑term goal is to make fully autonomous cleaning robots a reality.
  • Data collected during current remotely‑piloted cleanings will be used to develop more independent descendants.

#TauRobotics #HumanoidRobots #HomeCleaning #Robotics #AI

Source: I watched a humanoid robot clean my apartment. It felt like a taste of the future.

item.title: Tesla's Optimus and Google DeepMind's ALOHA 2 Advance General Purpose Robotics
item.description:
Tesla’s Optimus and Google DeepMind’s ALOHA 2 Advance General Purpose Robotics

Tesla’s Optimus and Google DeepMind’s ALOHA 2 are at the forefront of a potential revolution in robotics, aiming to bring human-like dexterity and general-purpose utility to machines through advanced AI. This development is part of a broader effort to use the same breakthroughs behind generative AI tools like ChatGPT to enable robots to imitate human movement in the physical world.

🔍 Overview

The robotics industry is currently projected to see massive growth, with Morgan Stanley estimating nearly 1 billion human-like robots by 2050, creating a market worth over $5 trillion. Marc Andreessen of Andreessen Horowitz has suggested that robotics could become the biggest industry in history. While some leaders like Jensen Huang of Nvidia predict human-level ability in robots could be reached this year, others remain skeptical about the difficulty of mastering the infinite variability of the physical world.

Robot Manufacturer Physical Form
Optimus Tesla Human-shaped (white with black head and torso)
ALOHA 2 Google DeepMind Two arms, grippers, and cameras

🧩 How it works

Progress in this field relies heavily on “robot policies,” which are AI systems that control how a general-purpose machine assesses its surroundings, plans movements, and performs tasks.

  • Generative AI Models: Proponents believe the same technology behind tools like ChatGPT and Claude will allow robots to imitate human movement.
  • Bimanual Teleoperation: Google DeepMind uses the ALOHA 2 hardware system to test its Gemini Robotics AI system.
  • Training by Example: Generalist robots like ALOHA 2 are trained to perform tasks based on specific examples provided to the AI.

⚙️ Key details

The two leading projects demonstrate different approaches to robot design and utility:

  • Tesla Optimus: Designed to automate human labor, including hauling sheet metal and folding laundry. It has been observed dancing, passing popcorn, vacuuming, and pressing microwave buttons, though it has also been seen falling or struggling with tasks like ironing.
  • Google DeepMind ALOHA 2: A non-humanoid “workhorse” for researchers. In testing, it has demonstrated the ability to pack a lunchbox by placing bread in a bag, putting grapes in a container, and zipping the lunchbox shut.
  • Humanoid vs. Generalist: There is an ongoing debate among roboticists about whether a human-like form is necessary for generalist robots or if simpler forms are more effective.

🚀 Availability

Elon Musk has stated that Optimus robots could eventually be produced for as little as $20,000 each. He predicted at the World Economic Forum in January that these robots could be on sale to the public by the end of 2027.

💡 Why it matters

If successful, these robots could automate almost all human labor in both factories and homes. However, researchers like Yann LeCun have expressed skepticism, arguing that current AI models based on language and images do not yet provide the intelligence necessary to make robots useful in the physical world. Jonathan Hurst of Agility Robotics notes that while creating a robot that looks like a person is easy, creating one that moves or behaves physically like a person is dramatically more difficult.

#Robotics #TeslaOptimus #GoogleDeepMind #GeminiRobotics #HumanoidRobots

Source: AI breakthroughs in robotics won’t change your life any time soon
